strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written paper that adapts attention-sink prefixing from LLM quantization to vision encoders, with the key insight that outlier/sink tokens in ViTs emerge in middle layers and are highly similar across images (cosine similarity 0.89), enabling pre-computed universal register caches.

Strong empirical analysis (Sec. 3): layerwise quantization sensitivity is convincingly linked to outlier emergence, and the foreground/background experiment (Fig. 3) plus the register-token comparison in Sec. J provide an interesting, well-supported explanation for why ViT outliers emerge later than LLM outliers (tokenization perspective).

Extensive evaluation across five diverse vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), multiple tasks (zero-shot classification, retrieval), multiple bitwidths, and multiple base PTQ methods (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, AWQ, QuaRot-based Hadamard rotation), demonstrating that RegCache is genuinely plug-and-play.

Honest and useful limitations discussion (hyperparameter tuning needs, per-model heuristics), computational overhead analysis (Sec. H shows negligible FLOPs change), comparison against the closely related test-time register approach of Jiang et al. (Tab. 14), and a simple supporting lemma for the universality observation (Appendix B).

Reported failures are not hidden: the DINOv2 setup shows a slight average degradation, and the ablation showing that single components can underperform the naive baseline is disclosed, which increases credibility.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' claim requires qualification: the method needs a reference task and reference dataset (ImageNet-1k training split, 50k images), and multiple hyperparameters (quantization-sensitive layer, number of prefix copies τ searched over 15 values, number of deleted tokens k̃, prefix-insertion layer) are tuned via validation. This is effectively hyperparameter optimization on a large in-domain dataset, and it is unclear how the procedure transfers to settings without an ImageNet-like reference set.

Practical gains in the practically relevant W8A8 regime are modest (e.g., +1.16 average for CLIP, and even negative for DINOv2). The largest improvements occur at W4A4/W6A6, but at W4A4 all methods remain near-zero accuracy, so the improved numbers (e.g., 21.50 vs 1.83) are still far from usable; the method's sweet spot is mainly 6-bit.

Generalization of the technique is uneven: DINOv2 degrades slightly, and the ablation (Tab. 6) shows each component alone can be worse than naive quantization, suggesting the method is sensitive to configuration and somewhat fragile rather than robustly beneficial.

Evaluation is limited to zero-shot classification and retrieval; the token-deletion step removes input-dependent tokens, whose effect on dense prediction tasks (segmentation, depth) or downstream multimodal pipelines is unexplored, despite the introduction motivating edge/robotic applications.

Novelty is incremental relative to Son et al. [31] (prefixing attention sinks for LLM quantization) and register-token literature [7, 14]; the contribution is mainly the adaptation to vision encoders plus supporting analysis, which reviewers may weigh differently depending on how much value they place on cross-domain transfer and the analysis itself.
Some experimental inconsistencies (e.g., FIMA-Q slightly degrades with RegCache on SigLIP2 in Tab. 8; CLIP/OpenCLIP latency increases ~5% due to prefixes) are acknowledged but only briefly discussed.

strengths: Interesting and well-supported empirical observations distinguishing vision encoders from LLMs: outlier tokens emerge in middle layers (rather than early layers), are highly similar across images (cosine similarity 0.89 vs 0.26 for normal tokens), and their appearance is linked to identifying semantically meaningless patches (Fig. 3, Sec. J). These observations are novel in the ViT quantization context and are plausibly useful beyond this paper.

The proposed RegCache method is technically reasonable and well-motivated: it adapts the LLM idea of prefixing attention sinks (PrefixQuant-style) to the ViT setting via middle-layer KV caching plus deletion of emergent sink tokens, with the ablation (Tab. 6) showing the two components are complementary.

Broad experimental coverage: five vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2) spanning contrastive and self-supervised training, four base PTQ algorithms plus naive RTN, three bitwidths, zero-shot classification and retrieval, weight-only quantization, and Hadamard-rotation-based methods. The comparison against test-time registers (Tab. 14) is a relevant and honest baseline.

Appendix includes useful supporting material: a simple theoretical explanation of high outlier-token cosine similarity (Lemma 1), FLOPs/latency analysis showing negligible overhead (<=0.2% FLOPs), visualization of searched registers, and sensitivity analysis of the prefix-insertion layer.

The paper is generally well written and clearly structured, with honest limitations discussion (hyperparameter tuning burden, per-encoder/per-quantizer heuristics) and a deliberate tokenization-perspective analysis (Sec. J) explaining LLM-vs-ViT differences.
weaknesses: The 'training-free' claim is overstated. RegCache requires selecting a quantization-sensitive layer via per-layer quantization sweeps, curating registers from 50,000 labeled ImageNet-1k training images, and searching tau in {1,...,15} and the number of deleted tokens against a labeled reference task. This is effectively a per-model, per-quantizer hyperparameter search on labeled data, which limits the plug-and-play framing and the practical appeal for arbitrary deployment scenarios.

Magnitude of gains depends heavily on pathological regimes. Large improvements occur mostly where base quantization collapses (e.g., Naive at W4A4/W6A6, or RepQ-ViT/SigLIP2 at W4A4: 0.40 -> 10.15), while W8A8 gains are typically <1 point and sometimes negative (e.g., DINOv2 W8A8 average gap -0.62). Since the motivating use case is compute-bound int8 inference, the practical benefit in the most relevant regime is modest, and the method fails outright on the self-supervised DINOv2 in some settings.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior work. The core mechanism (prefixing attention-sink tokens to absorb activation outliers) is directly borrowed from LLM quantization [31], and register tokens/their outlier behavior are established in [7, 14]; the contribution is primarily the adaptation (middle-layer insertion, caching, deletion) rather than a new algorithmic idea. The middle-layer finding, while nicely documented, mainly motivates where to insert rather than how.

Internal inconsistencies and reporting issues weaken confidence: the claimed A8A8 retrieval gap of -0.11 (CLIP) shows RegCache can hurt; Tab. 4 compares only Naive vs Naive+RegCache without reporting a comparable quantization baseline per dataset, making cross-dataset gains hard to interpret; the text states one baseline type was defined but then lists three; several claims (e.g., cost 'even decreases on average') rest on weak evidence.

Evaluation gaps for the deletion component: token deletion is justified via outlier tokens being background patches, but no dense-prediction or token-sensitive evaluation (e.g., segmentation, retrieval with patch pooling, OOD/background-dominated images) is provided to show that deleting top-k tokens is safe in general; only ImageNet-style zero-shot classification and MS-COCO retrieval are evaluated, and the deleted-token count is tuned per model.

Several design elements are heuristic and weakly justified: averaging KV caches over candidates (rather than selection or synthesis), searching 'up to three preceding blocks', the choice of reference task, and the k=100 candidate pool size all lack ablation or sensitivity analysis beyond the caching/deleting ablation.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written paper that identifies a genuine gap: existing attention-sink prefixing techniques for LLM quantization do not transfer directly to vision encoders because outlier tokens are input-dependent background patches rather than fixed special tokens.

The two technical innovations—middle-layer prefixing and token deletion—are grounded in careful empirical analysis (layerwise quantization sensitivity, foreground/background outlier emergence experiments, cross-image cosine similarity of outlier tokens, and a tokenization-perspective discussion in Sec. J), giving the method a solid analysis-to-design narrative.

RegCache is a simple, training-free, plug-in module with strong empirical support: five vision encoders spanning text-supervised and self-supervised training, three PTQ baselines plus FIMA-Q, AWQ, and QuaRot combinations, three bitwidths, and two downstream tasks (classification and retrieval), with consistent (often large) improvements, particularly at 4/6-bit.

Good breadth of supporting evidence: ablations showing synergy between caching and deleting, a comparison against the closest related method (test-time registers, Tab. 14), generalization checks of prefixes across datasets (Tab. 4), computational overhead analysis (Tab. 12), and honest reporting of negative cases (DINOv2-B/14 slight degradation).
The limitations section candidly acknowledges hyperparameter sensitivity and the heuristic nature of prefix/deletion token counts.
weaknesses: All evaluated models are base-scale (B/16, B/14); no larger encoders (e.g., L/14) are tested, so scalability of the observed outlier behavior and of the searched registers remains unverified—particularly relevant since the paper motivates the work by 'large-scale pretrained vision encoders.'

The method requires nontrivial search infrastructure: a 50k-image ImageNet-1k reference pool, layerwise sensitivity profiling, and a grid search over τ ∈ {1,...,15} and deletion count k̃ per model and per base quantizer. Although Tab. 4 shows prefix generalization, the per-configuration tuning weakens the claim of a 'go-to,' turnkey solution and raises mild overfitting concerns to the reference task.

Gains at W4A4 remain very small in absolute terms (often near 0–2% accuracy vs. FP32), and the one negative result (DINOv2-B/14) is not deeply analyzed; the ablation finding that a single component alone performs worse than naïve quantization suggests method fragility that deserves more discussion.

Some presentation inconsistencies reduce clarity: Table 2's FP32 row appears misaligned with the bitwidth columns, model naming is inconsistent (DINOv2-B/16 vs. B/14 across tables), and the baseline taxonomy in Sec. 5.1 lists only two of the promised three 'classes' of strategies.
Impact is primarily empirical; the theoretical explanation (Lemma 1) is a stylized asymptotic argument and does not predict when/why prefixing and deletion succeed or fail for a given encoder.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis: the paper establishes three findings (middle-layer localization of outliers, their cross-image universality with cosine similarity of 0.89, and a connection to quantization-sensitive layers) that are genuinely novel for large-scale vision encoders and distinguish the setting from LLMs, including a mechanistic tokenization-based explanation (Appendix M) and a supporting Lemma (Appendix F).
RegCache is a simple, training-free, plug-in module with negligible latency overhead (1.03-1.54%), which makes it practical and easily adoptable in existing PTQ pipelines.

Extensive and convincing experimental evidence: five diverse vision encoders (contrastive and self-supervised), five PTQ baselines across 4/6/8-bit settings, retrieval and 10 additional classification benchmarks, VLM evaluations (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA family) on image and video tasks, latency profiling with TensorRT, and ablations showing both components are necessary.

Careful validation of design choices, including a direct comparison with the concurrent test-time register approach [23] (Appendix B), a label-free reconstruction-loss-based selection alternative (Appendix K), combination with rotation-based (QuaRot) and weight-only (AWQ) methods, and dense-prediction analysis of token deletion (Appendix H).

Honest limitations section: the authors explicitly acknowledge hyperparameter sensitivity and the heuristic nature of prefix/deletion counts, and provide a label-free search variant that partially mitigates this.
weaknesses: Despite the 'training-free' claim, the method requires a validation-based search procedure on the ImageNet-1k training split (choosing the sensitive layer, k, tau via reference task accuracy), which is essentially a form of data-dependent tuning; the label-free alternative (Appendix K) works but with noticeably weaker and less consistent gains, which somewhat weakens the headline story.

Gains at W8A8 are often marginal (average deltas of +0.25 to +1.36), and in some DINOv2 settings RegCache actually hurts (e.g., -0.05 to -0.47), so the contribution is primarily valuable in the very low-bit regime; this scope should be made more explicit in the claims.

Experiments are limited to B/16 and B/14 scale encoders; there is no evidence on larger encoders (e.g., ViT-L/14 or So400m) that are increasingly common in modern VLMs, leaving scalability of the prefix/deletion strategy open.

Several hyperparameters (number of copied prefixes tau searched over 15 values, k up to three preceding blocks, deletion count k) are set heuristically per encoder/quantizer, raising reproducibility and transferability concerns for practitioners on new architectures, although the pipeline cost is reported to be low (~1 hour).

The method inserts/deletes tokens at inference, which changes the model's computation relative to the deployment model being quantized; while latency results mitigate this concern, the effect on downstream tasks requiring all tokens is only partially addressed (segmentation is covered in the appendix, but detection and other dense tasks are not).

strengths: The core insight—that outlier tokens in pretrained vision encoders emerge in middle layers, act as attention sinks, and are highly similar across images (cosine sim. 0.89 vs. 0.26 for normal tokens)—is clearly motivated and supported by a well-designed empirical study (layerwise sensitivity, FG/BG ablation with ImageNet-9, register-trained DINOv2 comparison in Sec. M).

RegCache is practical: it is training-free, requires only ~1 hour of search on a single GPU, adds negligible latency (<1.6%), and functions as a plug-in on top of five distinct PTQ baselines (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, ERQ), which is the appropriate evidence for an Algorithms/General contribution.

Experimental coverage is broad and convincing: five vision encoders, classification and retrieval, transfer to seven out-of-domain datasets (Tab. 5 mitigates ImageNet-1k overfitting concerns), VLM integration (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA) on image and video benchmarks, weight-only and Hadamard-rotation combinations, and a direct comparison against the closest prior work (test-time registers, Tab. 9).

Gains are most pronounced exactly where the method targets the problem (4-/6-bit settings), and the outlier-reduction analysis (Tab. 7) plus token-norm evidence connect the mechanism to the outcome rather than reporting unexplained improvements.
Limitations (hyperparameter sensitivity, per-encoder heuristic tuning) are candidly discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The method stacks several heuristics with dataset- and model-specific tuning: sensitivity-based layer selection, top-k candidate curation, prefix copy count τ searched over 1–15, and deletion count k̃, each tuned on the ImageNet-1k training split per encoder and per base quantizer. This weakens the 'universal register' narrative somewhat, since the method is partly a per-deployment calibration procedure, though Tab. 5 (K) partially addresses this.

Robustness of the evidence is uneven: DINOv2 shows average degradation (-0.47) at W8A8 and the two components alone can underperform the naive baseline (Tab. 8), suggesting the approach is fragile outside the regimes it was tuned for; a deeper characterization of failure modes would strengthen the paper.

At W8A8—the practically most relevant precision for compute-bound inference per the paper's own motivation—the gains over the strongest baseline (FIMA-Q) are small (typically <1 point), and FIMA-Q cannot even be run on DINOv2 (OOM), leaving the headline claims resting mainly on 4-/6-bit results.

Token deletion permanently removes spatially located tokens, which the main paper does not adequately address for dense prediction; the interpolation-based remedy appears only in the appendix (Sec. H), so the main-text method as described is not directly applicable to segmentation-style uses.

The contribution is an adaptation of the LLM attention-sink prefixing idea (PrefixQuant, Son et al.) to vision encoders; while the middle-layer prefixing and deletion are genuine and non-obvious modifications, the conceptual novelty is incremental and the paper would benefit from more formal grounding of why averaged KV caches transfer across images.

Reproducibility information is incomplete in the main text: code availability is not stated, and the interaction between hyperparameter choices (e.g., τ, k̃) and variance across reference-task splits is not reported (no error bars).

strengths: The paper makes a well-motivated empirical contribution: it carefully characterizes how activation outliers emerge in vision encoders (localized in middle-layer MLP projections, arising from semantically meaningless patches, and highly similar across images), which is a genuinely different phenomenon from LLM attention sinks. The analysis in Sec. 3 (layerwise sensitivity, FG/BG-only experiments, cosine-similarity of outlier tokens, and the tokenization hypothesis in Appendix M comparing DINOv2 with/without registers against LLaMA) is insightful and goes beyond just presenting a method.

The proposed RegCache method is novel and sensible: instead of learned registers (Darcet et al.) or test-time registers (Jiang et al.), it precomputes KV caches of register candidate tokens from reference images and prefixes them only in the middle-to-final layers, combined with token deletion of internally emerging outliers. The comparison with test-time registers (Table 9) directly validates the design choice.

Extensive and convincing experimental evidence: five vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2) spanning contrastive and self-supervised training, five distinct PTQ baseline families, three bit-widths (4/6/8-bit), standalone classification and retrieval, seven transfer datasets, and VLM deployments (Qwen3-VL 2B/8B, LLaVA family) on image, video, and multi-domain reasoning benchmarks. Gains are largest exactly where they matter most (4-bit), e.g., +27.48 (Best Δ) for SigLIP2-W4A4 on ImageNet and consistent gains on LLaVA/Qwen3-VL.

Practicality is well supported: the method is training-free, plug-in, adds only ~1.5% latency (Table 6), generalizes across datasets (Table 5), and includes a label-free variant based on reconstruction loss (Appendix K) plus combinations with weight-only quantization, Hadamard rotations, and LLM-style outlier methods (Appendices N-P).

The ablation (Table 8) is informative: each component alone can be worse than naive, but combined they work, showing the two mechanisms are complementary and non-obvious. Limitations (hyperparameter tuning, heuristics) are honestly stated.
The paper is clearly written with a logical structure from observation to hypothesis to method, and the supplementary material is thorough.
weaknesses: The method relies on several tuned hyperparameters (number of prefix tokens τ, number of deleted tokens k̃, candidate set size k, insertion layer), searched using the ImageNet-1k training split as a reference task. Although a label-free reconstruction-loss alternative is provided (Appendix K), its results are noticeably weaker in some cases (e.g., CLIP W4A4 with FIMA-Q: 62.27 vs. 62.08 label-based, but SigLIP W4A4 drops from 78.48 to 76.12), so the strongest results still depend on task-based validation. This somewhat weakens the 'fully training-free, plug-and-play' narrative.

Gains are not uniform: for the strongest baseline (ERQ) at W8A8 on DINOv2, RegCache slightly degrades accuracy (Best Δ -0.05, Average Δ -0.47), and improvements at W8A8 are often modest. The method's benefits are mostly concentrated in the 4-bit regime and on models with very large outlier norms (SigLIP2, DINOv2), so the scope of the contribution should be understood as low-bit/strong-outlier settings.

The theoretical explanation for the universality of outlier tokens (Lemma 1 in Appendix F) is a simple spiked-vector argument; it explains the observed cosine similarity but does not provide a deeper account of why outlier tokens emerge in middle layers specifically. The tokenization hypothesis in Appendix M is suggestive but remains a hypothesis with limited evidence (one model pair, layer-1/2 histograms).

Some heuristics are not deeply justified, e.g., averaging the KV caches of candidate tokens to compose the register, and searching up to three preceding blocks for candidate sets; the sensitivity of results to these design details could be examined more.

The evaluation is limited to ViT-B-scale encoders; it is unclear how the approach scales to larger vision encoders (e.g., ViT-L/H, SigLIP-SO400M) where outlier behavior may differ, and where prefixing and deletion strategies might interact differently.

No declared contribution type is given; under the default Algorithms/General category the paper is a solid applied-algorithm contribution rather than a foundational one, which is consistent with the assessment above.
